why.Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments: When you want to skip the loose, steep scree of Aasgard Pass, or the day is hot and you prefer a shaded, gentler grade, accepting a longer walk and more gain.

review.notes: Both approaches are in common use; Aasgard is the shorter, steeper line, Snow Lakes the longer, gradual and shaded one.

why.Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments: When Aasgard Pass or the Stuart Lake trailhead is unavailable, or to avoid the loose headwall for a gentler grade, at the cost of a longer walk and more gain.

review.notes: Same two approaches as the other Prusik routes; stored notes name the fallback use.

why.Aasgard Pass with snow, early season: Early season, May to early July, while the pass holds continuous snow; quicker than talus but needs an axe, sometimes crampons, and has avalanche and hidden-creek hazard.
why.Snow Lakes and the lower Enchantments to: To avoid the steep, loose headwall of Aasgard Pass, or on a hot day when you want shade and a gentler grade, accepting more distance and gain.

review.notes: Aasgard in dry conditions is the usual line; the snow variant is the same route earlier in the year.

why.Eightmile Creek, Eightmile Pass and the: When you prefer the shorter map distance from a lower trailhead and accept a long day of trail first; check whether fire closures affect the trail beyond the East Fork junction.

review.notes: Search evidence calls Eightmile-Hidden Lakes the main approach to Ptarmigan and Slate Pass/Shellrock a Lost Peak base-camp route; this contradicts the stored mark.

problems: Stored primary is the Shellrock Pass camp (Slate Pass road end), but search evidence suggests the Eightmile Creek / Hidden Lakes approach is the standard one for Ptarmigan Peak. Mark not changed; owner to review.

why.From the Libby Creek road and Trail #415: When you prefer a shorter walk to the crest from the Libby Creek side and accept one very loose gully; wear a helmet.

review.notes: Libby gully described as steep and loose; Crater side SE ridge avoids avalanche terrain.

why.From the Crater Creek road and the lake: When you want to avoid the loose, confined gully, or snow still lies in it, and accept more off-trail ridge travel on the south-east side.

review.notes: Libby gully is the named standard; the Crater side is the gully-avoiding alternative.

why.Chewuch River trail to Remmel Lake: When you want an easier, better-kept trail than the burned, blowdown-prone Andrews Creek valley, and can spend a night along the river to break up the walk.

review.notes: Search suggests the Chewuch River approach is the commonly used one and Andrews Creek is lesser used due to fire damage; this contradicts the stored mark.

problems: Stored primary is Andrews Creek, but evidence suggests the Chewuch River approach is more commonly used (the Andrews Creek trail is burned and avoided by many). Mark not changed; owner to review.

why.Williams Lake and War Creek Ridge: When you want a longer, scenic outing on good trail instead of the brushy creek bushwhack, or an overnight or loop with a neighbouring summit, camping at the lake.

review.notes: Reynolds Creek is the usual route; Williams Creek is the longer overnight alternative.

why.Car-to-car day push: When you could not get a permit for Sahale Glacier Camp, or want to skip the quota; a strong party can do it in one long day, carrying glacier gear the whole way.

review.notes: Both the camp and the single long day are in regular use.

why.Downey Creek and the south end of the tr: When working the Ptarmigan Traverse from the south end, or linking Sentinel into it, after a long walk up Downey Creek and several days of off-trail and glacier travel.

review.notes: Evidence confirms Sentinel is reached along the traverse via Le Conte Glacier; the Downey Creek reason rests on traverse context and stored notes.
fromStoredNotes: Downey Creek and the south end of the traverse

why.Boston Basin to the SE Ridge notch — lat: Late season, August to September, once the approach gully has melted out to loose scree; expect rockfall risk from parties above and a moat at the glacier edge.

review.notes: Sources say the gully is snow early and scree later; neither is clearly more common, so the stored mark is left.

why.Camp at the bench, summit the second day: When you would rather not do the whole climb in one long day: camp at the bench, cross the glacier on firm morning snow, and be back over the col before afternoon softening.

review.notes: Evidence says most parties do it as an overnight, a single day being for very fit parties; contradicts the stored mark.

problems: Stored primary is the day push, but sources say most people do Silver Star as an overnight at the bench and only very fit parties do it in a day. Mark not changed; owner to review.
